papers.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
papers.tldr: A fixed set of prompt-independent steering vectors added to the block outputs of a frozen diffusion transformer recovers 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models with 65x fewer parameters than the RL LoRA, so most RL post-training gain behaves like a constant activation shift.
summary: RL post-training clearly improves text rendering, composition and visual quality in diffusion transformers, and these skills look prompt-dependent, so one would expect RL to learn complex input-dependent changes. Nobody had checked how much of the gain a single input-independent shift could explain.

The authors attach one constant steering vector per block output of the frozen base model (0.29M parameters on SD3.5-M versus 18.8M for the RL-tuned LoRA). They fit these vectors to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints with no reward in the loss, and separately train them from zero with online RL. The same vectors are used for every prompt, token and sampling seed, and they test six RL-tuned image models and two RL-tuned video models.

The distilled vectors recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains on the six image models and 89.8% and 111.9% on the two video models. Trained directly with online RL, the vectors alone beat weight-based RL on OCR text rendering and PickScore on SD3.5-M. Takeaway for steering-geometry work: RL fine-tuning of generative models may be largely a global translation in activation space, which gives a cheap baseline and a diagnostic (fit a constant shift, measure recovered reward) for any fine-tuning method you want to explain. Caveat: results are on diffusion transformers and reward metrics only; whether the same holds for LLM RLHF is not tested here.

papers.title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.tldr: DualSAE adds a decorrelated residual branch next to a standard SAE so the sparse code keeps the semantics while the residual handles leftover reconstruction, giving about 29% better reconstruction and 34% better monosemanticity on average.
summary: In a standard SAE the same sparse code has to both reconstruct activations faithfully and be interpretable, and the two goals can pull against each other. Pushing sparsity for interpretability usually costs reconstruction, and vice versa.

DualSAE keeps a normal SAE as a Sparse Branch and adds a plug-in Residual Branch that models non-semantic information the sparse code leaves out. A decorrelation loss keeps the two branches from overlapping in what they reconstruct, and a two-stage schedule first stabilizes the sparse code before coupling in the residual branch. They test many encoder-SAE combinations on two vision datasets and two language corpora.

Across configurations DualSAE gives mean relative gains of about 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in monosemanticity score, and improves downstream topic modeling, hypothesis generation and LLM steering. Qualitative checks suggest the residual branch indeed holds non-semantic content. Takeaway: if you report SAE reconstruction error as a faithfulness measure, a residual branch can hide what the sparse code misses, so evaluate the sparse branch on its own; the design is easy to bolt onto existing SAEs and code is released (github.com/AtlasAnalyticsLab/DualSAE). Caveat: the abstract reports relative averages only, not per-model numbers or comparisons with error-node or crosscoder approaches.

papers.title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
papers.tldr: SAE features from GraphCast show that a causally important feature can lack physical meaning, and scaling up convection-associated features cut tropical-cyclone intensity error by a median 51% over seven storms.
summary: AI weather forecasters are used in high-stakes settings, so it matters whether they rely on sound mechanisms. A common assumption in interpretability is that the features that matter causally are the ones with clean physical semantics, which has not been tested in weather models.

The authors train sparse autoencoders on GraphCast, the DeepMind autoregressive forecaster, and run ablations and feature-scaling interventions on the activations during rollout. They test a feature tied to the model's computational mesh and features associated with convection and low-level vorticity during tropical-cyclone intensification.

Ablating the mesh-locked feature raises global geopotential height error even though it has no conventional physical meaning. Suppressing convection and vorticity features weakens predicted cyclone deepening, while amplifying them lowers intensity error, with a median 51% error reduction across seven storms for convection features. Takeaway: causal relevance and human-readable meaning are separate properties, so SAE audits of medical or scientific models should test features by intervention rather than trusting labels. Caveat: the steering result covers only seven storms and one model.

papers.title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
papers.tldr: Comparing linear probes with model answers across six base/post-trained model pairs shows post-training mainly changes how a judgment is read out, not what is represented: answer sensitivity dropped (mean delta d' = -0.34) on human-vs-AI text judgments while probes still separated the classes.
summary: When a model answers badly, it is unclear whether it lacks the information or fails to use it. Post-training (SFT, RLHF) could change either the representation or its readout, and these are usually not separated.

The study compares linear probes against the models' own answers using signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. The main task is judging whether German texts were human- or AI-written; a reproducible public case uses the truth of negated statements. Stage-wise checkpoints, model stitching and a fine-tuning study with 2,000 added labeled authorship judgments locate where the change happens.

On authorship, probes separated the classes well while answers did not and often reversed them; post-training lowered answer sensitivity by d' -0.34 across families. On negation, probes decoded truth near ceiling in every model and post-training repaired the base models' failure to use it. The change appeared during SFT and, from mid-depth on, sat at positions after the text. Takeaway: probe accuracy says little about behavior, so pair probes with answer-level analysis; a small training signal can set the readout direction. Caveat: the main corpora cannot be shared, so only the negation case is reproducible.

papers.title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
papers.tldr: Complete Path Contribution decomposes a network's output exactly into contributions of individual input-to-output paths, with an algorithm that finds the k strongest paths in time empirically linear in k, exposing excitatory-inhibitory interactions in image classifiers and a retina model.
summary: Circuit analyses usually measure pairwise interactions between units, heads or layers and then stitch them together. That misses higher-order interactions along whole causal chains, so questions such as whether inhibitory paths veto excitatory ones cannot be answered.

The method splits the network output into mathematically complete contributions from individual paths, and partial sums give complete contributions for circuits at any granularity. An efficient search returns the top-k paths without enumerating the exponential number of paths. They apply it to benchmark image classification networks and to an interpretable model of the mouse retina responding to natural stimuli.

In image classifiers the method quantifies how excitatory and inhibitory pathways combine to produce decisions, and in the retina model it shows dynamic receptive fields emerging from excitatory-inhibitory motifs between cell types. Takeaway: completeness at every granularity makes this a candidate for faithful explanations of CNN-based medical models, where gradient attribution is not complete. Caveat: the abstract gives no quantitative comparison with attribution baselines and does not report results on transformers or LLMs.

papers.title: SRED: Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation Across Magnifications in Whole-Slide Imaging
papers.tldr: An SAE learns an "event dictionary" from 20x pathology features, and a 5x encoder is distilled to predict which events occur in each region, improving macro-F1 by 1.1 points and C-index by 1.7 points over native 5x features at 5x cost.
summary: High-magnification whole-slide analysis keeps detail but needs many patches, while low magnification is cheap but loses detail. Existing cross-magnification distillation tries to match features that the low-magnification input cannot actually see, and some methods need slide-level labels.

SRED trains a sparse autoencoder on 20x teacher features to get a dictionary of events, then uses logical OR pooling to record whether each event appears in any aligned 20x patch within a 5x region. A pretrained 5x encoder is fine-tuned to predict these regional event targets, without slide-level labels. Evaluation covers seven classification and grading cohorts and five survival cohorts.

Against native 5x features, SRED raises average macro-F1 by 1.1 points and average C-index by 1.7 points, with runtime equal to 5x and an average 11.58x speedup over 20x. Some dictionary components respond to recognizable histological patterns. Takeaway: SAE codes can serve as compact, label-free distillation targets, an idea that could transfer to compressing heavy ultrasound or pathology encoders. Caveat: gains are modest, and the paper is a CVPR 2027 submission, not yet peer reviewed.

papers.title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Label-free persona and knowledge directions for lie detection, tested up to Llama-3.3-70B on Liars' Bench, transfer better than single-dataset probes on three of four models, but many gains stay inside a random-direction control band.
summary: Linear probes are cheap lie detectors but often fail across kinds of lies. Label-free directions from honest versus deceptive role-play had not been tested at 70B scale or on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can use identical words.

The authors extend a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts, and take the persona direction at each model's middle layer. They also build a knowledge direction contrasting answerable and unanswerable questions followed by the same scripted denial, and compare everything against supervised probes and a band of random directions on four models.

The persona direction ranks lies better than single-dataset probes on three of four models but fails on Qwen; on Llama-3.3-70B its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. The knowledge direction separates lies from identical honest denials on two models, narrowly on a third, and not on the fourth. The sum of both beats a same-depth supervised probe on all four models, but trails it on held-out lies. Takeaway: the random-direction control band is a useful sanity check for any concept-direction claim, and many direction results here are fragile. Caveat: mixed results that depend on model and benchmark wording.

papers.title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
papers.source: arXiv cs.SD, NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability for Discovery
papers.tldr: Circuit discovery with the Auto-Emergence algorithm finds a sparse sub-network in ChatMusician and MuPT that drives prediction of the closing tonic in I...V->I progressions, confirmed by causal intervention.
summary: Circuit discovery is well developed for language models but almost untested in music models. It is unknown whether musically meaningful functions, such as resolving a harmonic progression, are carried by identifiable sub-networks.

The authors study two symbolic music generators, ChatMusician and MuPT, on predicting the terminal tonic root in the classical I...V->I pattern. They use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network and validate it with causal interventions.

Interventions show the found circuit is a primary driver of the harmonic progression behavior, and the authors describe this as the first systematic circuit discovery study in music. Takeaway: a clean example of moving circuit methods to a new domain with a well-defined target behavior, a template for domain models such as medical encoders. Caveat: a workshop paper (accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability for Discovery per the arXiv comment) on one musical pattern, and the abstract gives no quantitative faithfulness numbers.

papers.title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
papers.tldr: Visa Research fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B on billions of labeled tabular rows and report it beats a range of tabular classifiers and their production deep model, with ablations pointing to the first two FFN layers.
summary: Prior work often finds LLMs trail tree models and tabular-specific networks on large tabular classification. Whether a pretrained LLM can win at industrial scale was unclear.

They fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B on billions of rows of labeled tabular data, describing data preparation, serialization, training recipe, design ablations and deployment validation. They also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and run interpretability and component-ablation experiments.

The fine-tuned model is reported to outperform many tabular classifiers and Visa's production deep learning model; interpretability results suggest feature-specific associations, and ablations implicate the earliest two FFN layers in making task information linearly decodable. Takeaway: at very large data scale a small LLM with a careful serialization recipe can compete with tabular specialists, a useful counterpoint for TabPFN-style small-data comparisons. Caveat: the abstract gives no numbers, the data is proprietary, and the report is marked work in progress.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Feature Representations and Pretrained Tabular Foundation Models for Generalizable Melt Pool Geometry Prediction
papers.tldr: On small laser powder bed fusion datasets, TabPFN, TabDPT and TabICLv2 generally beat classical models at melting-mode classification, and physics-based dimensionless features give the biggest gain in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96).
summary: Manufacturing datasets are small and process-property relations shift across materials, so models trained on raw process parameters transfer poorly. It is unclear whether tabular foundation models or better features help more in this small-data regime.

The study compares raw parameters with two dimensionless features (normalized enthalpy and Peclet number) and benchmarks four classical models (Gaussian process, SVM, random forest, XGBoost) against three tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, TabICLv2). Tasks are melt pool width and depth regression and melting-mode classification on 316L, IN625, IN718 and combined-material data.

Dimensionless features match or beat raw parameters in most settings, with the largest gain in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96), and the tabular foundation models generally classify better than classical baselines, especially on multi-material data. Takeaway: a fair small-data benchmark of three current tabular FMs that also shows domain-informed feature engineering still matters alongside them. Caveat: a narrow application with small datasets, and the abstract gives no per-model numbers for the FM comparison.

papers.title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
papers.tldr: PriTabICL makes private demonstrations for tabular in-context learning by clustering records under DP and synthesizing each cluster with a prediction-focused workload; its PrivSyn version beats global PrivSyn in 8 of 12 settings.
summary: Tabular in-context learning puts real labeled records in the prompt, which leaks personal data. Adding DP noise directly distorts feature-label relations, and synthesizing one global DP dataset can wash out local structure and minority patterns.

PriTabICL partitions records into DP clusters, synthesizes each cluster separately with an existing DP synthesis algorithm, and uses a fixed feature-target workload to spend privacy budget on prediction-relevant statistics. At inference each query is routed to a cluster and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic data, with no extra privacy cost. Experiments use four real-world datasets.

PriTabICL-PrivSyn improves over global PrivSyn in 8 of 12 settings and beats existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all settings, and code is released. Takeaway: for in-context tabular models (LLM-based here, but the idea applies to TabPFN-style contexts), cluster-wise, task-aligned synthetic context is a practical way to share private clinical tables. Caveat: only four datasets, and the evaluation is with LLM prompting rather than dedicated tabular foundation models.

papers.title: Development and validation of a TRUS-based prostate cancer prediction model with PSAD stratification in a two-center Western Chinese cohort: a retrospective cohort study with cost-effectiveness analysis.
papers.tldr: A logistic regression model combining transrectal ultrasound findings with stratified PSA density reached AUC 0.915 (training) and 0.943 (validation) in 767 men, and a high threshold avoided 47.0% of biopsies.
summary: PSA screening has low positive predictive value where prostate cancer incidence is low, which leads to many unnecessary biopsies. MRI pathways are not always available, so cheaper triage based on TRUS is of interest in resource-limited settings.

This two-center retrospective study included 767 men with PSA of at least 4 ng/ml (558 training, 209 validation). PSA density was split into five categories, and a logistic regression model was built from clinical and TRUS features; four screening strategies were compared for cost-effectiveness.

Five predictors were selected: age, PSAD category, extraprostatic extension, solid hypoechoic lesions and unclear boundary. Discrimination was 0.915 in training and 0.943 in validation with good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.57), and the high-threshold strategy (at least 0.5) avoided 47.0% of biopsies at the lowest total cost. Takeaway: reader-scored TRUS signs plus PSAD form a strong non-AI baseline that any deep model on conventional TRUS should beat. Caveat: retrospective, hand-crafted features with no deep learning, and the authors say it is not suitable for population screening or as a replacement for MRI pathways.
